items.title: Topic statistics and libstatistics_collector removed from rclcpp in Rolling (Makoa Mata-mata)
items.summary: Hi everyone, Heads-up about an API removal that recently landed in Rolling and will be part of ROS 2 Makoa Mata-mata (May 23, 2027): built-in topic statistics have been removed from rclcpp , and libstatistics_collector is no longer part of the ROS 2 core. What changed The following PRs were merged on October 5, 2026: ros2/rclcpp#3203 : removes the topic statistics implementation from rclcpp , rclcpp_lifecycle and rclcpp_components ros2/ros2#1878 : removes libstatistics_collector from ros2.repos ros2/demos#812 : removes the topic_statistics_demo package ros2/examples#476 : removes the MinimalSubscriberWithTopicStatistics example ros2/ros2_documentation#7245 : removes the topic statistics tutorial and concept pages from the Rolling docs Why Hardly anyone was using it. Recent bug reports suggested the feature saw very little real-world use. There’s a better way to get this data. At ROSCon we discussed providing an interface so a third-party package could plug the old behavior back in. We decided not to: tooling that hooks into the existing tracepoints (tracetools / ros2_tracing ) can collect the same information without adding code and cost to every subscription. Faster builds. rclcpp
items.articleText: Topic statistics and libstatistics_collector removed from rclcpp in Rolling (Makoa Mata-mata) - Projects - Open Robotics Discourse Topic statistics and libstatistics_collector removed from rclcpp in Rolling (Makoa Mata-mata) Projects rclcpp , rolling , makoa ahcorde November 3, 2026, 1:20pm 1 Hi everyone, Heads-up about an API removal that recently landed in Rolling and will be part of ROS 2 Makoa Mata-mata (May 23, 2027): built-in topic statistics have been removed from rclcpp , and libstatistics_collector is no longer part of the ROS 2 core. What changed The following PRs were merged on October 5, 2026: ros2/rclcpp#3203 : removes the topic statistics implementation from rclcpp , rclcpp_lifecycle and rclcpp_components ros2/ros2#1878 : removes libstatistics_collector from ros2.repos ros2/demos#812 : removes the topic_statistics_demo package ros2/examples#476 : removes the MinimalSubscriberWithTopicStatistics example ros2/ros2_documentation#7245 : removes the topic statistics tutorial and concept pages from the Rolling docs Why Hardly anyone was using it. Recent bug reports suggested the feature saw very little real-world use. There’s a better way to get this data. At ROSCon we discussed providing an interface so a third-party package could plug the old behavior back in. We decided not to: tooling that hooks into the existing tracepoints (tracetools / ros2_tracing ) can collect the same information without adding code and cost to every subscription. Faster builds. rclcpp no longer depends on libstatistics_collector and statistics_msgs , and fewer templates end up in every subscription. Compiling a simple node with one publisher and one subscription went from 6.32 s to 4.91 s (about 22% faster, measured on a Ryzen 9900X). Overall, the change removes around 2,400 lines of code. Am I affected? Only if you use the C++ topic statistics API. In that case your code will no longer compile against Rolling . These are removed: Removed Where NodeOptions::enable_topic_statistics() (getter and setter) rclcpp/node_options.hpp SubscriptionOptions::topic_stats_options (TopicStatisticsOptions : state , publish_topic , publish_period , qos ) rclcpp/subscription_options.hpp rclcpp::TopicStatisticsState rclcpp/topic_statistics_state.hpp rclcpp::topic_statistics::SubscriptionTopicStatistics rclcpp/topic_statistics/subscription_topic_statistics.hpp NodeBaseInterface::get_enable_topic_statistics_default() , and the enable_topic_statistics_default argument of the NodeBase constructor rclcpp/node_interfaces/ The enable_topic_statistics extra argument when loading a component rclcpp_components Note that the last two items also affect you if you implement your own NodeBaseInterface , or if your launch files pass enable_topic_statistics as an extra argument to a composable node. Also, nothing publishes on the /statistics topic anymore. Tools or dashboards that subscribe to it will stop receiving data. The statistics_msgs message package itself is not removed. It lives in rcl_interfaces , so existing tools that use those messages keep building. How to migrate Remove the API calls listed above. For most users that’s deleting options.topic_stats_options.state = rclcpp::TopicStatisticsState::Enable; (or .enable_topic_statistics(true) ) and the related includes. Collect statistics from tracepoints instead. rclcpp already emits tracepoints on every publish and every subscription callback, which give you message rates, periods and latencies without changing your nodes: ros2_tracing to record traces and analyze them offline. Community tools built on the same instrumentation are already appearing. For example, ros2_pulse reports live topic rates, can export to Prometheus and Grafana, and can even publish statistics_msgs on /statistics if you have tooling that depends on it. Need it on older distros? Nothing changes for Humble, Jazzy, Kilted or Lyrical: topic statistics are still there. The removal only applies to Rolling and to Makoa Mata-mata onwards. Feedback welcome During review, @tomoyafujita raised good points: whether this should have gone through a deprecation period first, and whether a longer-term statistics hook should live at the rcl level, so rclpy and other client libraries, plus services and actions, could share one mechanism. We went with a direct removal because the feature had so few users and we’re early in the Makoa cycle, which leaves plenty of time to react before the release. If you depend on topic statistics in production, please reply here. We’d like to hear what you’re using it for, so we can point you to the right replacement or document a migration path. Thanks to @jmachowinski for driving this cleanup, and to everyone who reviewed it and joined the discussion at ROSCon. items.title: Microduck ROS 2 Integration: Running Policies in MuJoCo with ROS 2
items.summary: Hi everyone! I’ve been working on bringing Microduck into the ROS 2 ecosystem , and I’m excited to share that the integration is now open source! GitHub: GitHub - Arjunros/microduck_ros2: ROS 2 simulation, skills, Nav2 navigation and LLM/voice control for Pollen Robotics' Microduck biped, in MuJoCo with the real BAM actuator model · GitHub What does it do? The integration allows Microduck policies to run in MuJoCo while exposing the simulated robot through standard ROS 2 interfaces. Some of the key features include: Policy execution: Runs existing policies from microduck-policies without modifying the original policies. Actuator simulation: Uses the BAM XL330 actuator model. Observation validation: Verified observations against infer_policy.py with an error tolerance of 1e-6. ROS 2 interfaces: /cmd_vel for velocity commands Joint states IMU data TF and URDF Head camera feed, visualized in RViz Skill integration: Existing skills such as kicks, roulade, ground pick, and sit/stand are exposed as ROS 2 services. Manifest compatibility: Skill execution follows the rules defined in the robot’s manifest, consistent with robotd behavior. Why this integration? The goal is to make Microduck

items.articleText: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too Simon Willison’s Weblog Newsletter Sponsored by: Greptile — Your code reviewer uses Computer Use to catch bugs by opening your app and clicking through it. Now you can configure its test environment and define the key user journeys it tests. Try it for free Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too 3rd November 2026 Yesterday’s hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Weight-Space Programming Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models. spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use. I’m going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two. The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games—Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it’s an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question: The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response. The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games: breakout/prompt.txt freeway/prompt.txt pacman/prompt.txt pong/prompt.txt I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others. Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this: llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \ -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here’s what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro , which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens. But how about Qwen 3.8 27B ? That’s still my favorite model to run on my own laptop—it’s just 17GB (I use this version ) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025. I fired up LM Studio , ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command: LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \ llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \ -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b (I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue .) After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here’s the reasoning trace ): Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets. Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards. Confidence: 72% This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong (reasoning ) in 1h 4m 54s: Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object. Description: The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized. Confidence: 75% And Breakout (reasoning ) in 52m 25s: Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game. Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty. Confidence: 88% Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn’t surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here’s that transcript —Qwen thought it was “A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally”. The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here’s a sample: What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let’s list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right? That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort. It’s a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I’ve seen around it does not feel justified. I’m not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways. items.title: macOS 27 does not support CoreStorage volumes
items.articleText: Contents Details Workaround Call for better workarounds macOS 15 Sequoia had a hard time with CoreStorage – and thus encrypted HFS+ volumes – since it deprecated both technologies and callously crippled some important tools for working with them, but nonetheless it mostly still worked. While I’d often – but not always – have to manually unlock one of my HFS+ volumes – but not the others – at boot, and it also refused to convert some – but not all – volumes from HFS+ to APFS1 , keeping me trapped in the situation – it ultimately still worked . I could get at my data and use the volumes more or less normally. Unfortunately, in macOS 27 that’s no longer the case. Not only does Golden Gate just not support CoreStorage / encrypted HFS+ volumes, out of the box you can’t do anything with them – can’t mount them, can’t convert them to APFS, can’t even erase them. It renders your expensive storage hardware completely useless. Worse, macOS 27 puts up a misleading dialog, upon boot, saying that macOS 28 (the next version) won’t support these volumes. I have no idea what Apple’s doing or thinking. Maybe it’s all just an embarrassing misunderstanding – the file system team told the notifications team that CoreStorage & encrypted HFS+ support is going away, and typoed the version number as 28 rather than 27? Details macOS 27 cannot mount CoreStorage volumes automatically or through any normal means. Worse, Disk Utility can’t mount them even when manually told to – it just fails with the cryptic error: com.apple.DiskManagement.disenter error 49,153 diskutil mount also fails, this time with an error message that is a blatant lie: disk27 is a CoreStorage Logical Volume which is locked; use "diskutil coreStorage unlockVolume" $ diskutil cs unlockVolume BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D is already unlocked and is attached as disk27 $ diskutil cs list CoreStorage logical volume groups (1 found) | +-- Logical Volume Group 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB ========================================================= Name: Smash Status: Online Size: 2000054960128 B (2.0 TB) Free Space: 0 B (0 B) | +-< Physical Volume 1B5A1754-184B-4F17-A797-BF69B4BB627F | ---------------------------------------------------- | Index: 0 | Disk: disk10s2 | Status: Online | Size: 2000054960128 B (2.0 TB) | +-> Logical Volume Family 376204CD-8048-4962-B05C-72F4FC16B77B ---------------------------------------------------------- Encryption Type: AES-XTS Encryption Status: Unlocked Conversion Status: Complete High Level Queries: Fully Secure | Passphrase Required | Accepts New Users | Has Visible Users | Has Volume Key | +-> Logical Volume BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D --------------------------------------------------- Disk: disk27 Status: Online Size (Total): 1999702634496 B (2.0 TB) Revertible: No LV Name: Smash Volume Name: Smash Content Hint: Apple_HFS Tangentially: surprisingly, hfsutils (installed via brew ) don’t work at all: $ sudo hmount /dev/disk27 hmount: /dev/disk27: not a Macintosh HFS volume (Invalid argument) $ sudo hmount /dev/disk10s2 hmount: /dev/disk10s2: not a Macintosh HFS volume (Invalid argument) But what’s even worse about this dumpster fire is that macOS 27 can mount these volumes just fine – it’s just that all the normal ways to do it are completely broken. If you go down to a lower level and run mount_hfs directly, it does work: $ sudo mkdir -p /Volumes/Smash $ sudo mount_hfs -o rdonly /dev/disk27 /Volumes/Smash $ ls /Volumes/Smash Documents Pictures Scratch space That said… that -o rdonly parameter… in principle it shouldn’t be required, but I could not get macOS 27 to let me mount any HFS-on-CoreStorage volume as read-write – no matter what I did, it always fails with error “Resource busy” (EBUSY). I spent a lot of time trying to debug this, and could find no evidence of anything having the volume in question open (nothing in lsof etc). But wait, it gets worse. macOS 27 can’t even erase the volume. All the normal tools – diskutil , Disk Utility, etc – fail with that same “Resource busy” error. Workaround Thankfully, with the help of Gemini 4 Argon, I did find a workaround. It’s convoluted, but takes only a few steps, thankfully. First, while if you try to delete the logical volume group it ostensibly fails, it doesn’t completely fail – it does actually delete the logical volume(s) within: $ diskutil cs delete 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB Started CoreStorage operation Unmounting Logical Volumes Destroying Logical Volume Group Erasing disk10s2 newfs_hfs: cannot create filesystem on /dev/rdisk10s2: Resource busy Mounting disk Could not mount disk10s2 after erase Error: -69832: File system formatter failed 1 💣 $ diskutil cs list CoreStorage logical volume groups (1 found) | +-- Logical Volume Group 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB ========================================================= Name: Smash Status: Offline Size: 2000054960128 B (2.0 TB) Free Space: -none- | +-< Physical Volume 1B5A1754-184B-4F17-A797-BF69B4BB627F ---------------------------------------------------- (No properties) $ diskutil cs delete 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB Started CoreStorage operation Destroying Logical Volume Group Error: -69783: Unable to delete the CoreStorage Logical Volume Group You still can’t destroy it completely, nor can you erase the physical volume yet – the “Resource busy” errors persist. But, the trick is to restart – after that, you can then erase the volume. So it seems that whatever broken thing is holding the physical volume (or logical volume group) in a ‘busy’ state is tied to the existence of the logical volume(s) therein, and once they’re deleted (and the machine rebooted) the bug stops being triggered. Call for better workarounds I’ve glossed over a lot of debugging and attempts I made to save the volume in-place, by either making it work as-is (even if only with e.g. hfsutils) or by converting it to APFS, but neither I nor Gemini 4 Argon could find anything that worked. It’s too late for me – I was forced to just delete all my HFS+ & CoreStorage volumes and rebuild them painstakingly from backups – but if anyone finds a way, I’d love to amend this post, for the benefit of future readers. The problem remains the same in macOS 27 – so three major macOS versions, at a minimum, where essential system update functionality has not worked. Sigh. $ diskutil apfs convert disk27 Converting the volume on disk27 to an APFS Volume on an APFS Container Started APFS operation on disk27 (Smash) Converting HFS Volume to an APFS Container which will export one APFS Volume The target is the Journaled HFS+ volume "Smash" on disk27 backed via CoreStorage on disk10s2 Checking booter partition disk10s3 The target is a data disk; it is not a macOS system disk No APFS EFI driver found to install Saving encryption context The target is encrypted Unmounting disk27 Starting conversion from HFS to APFS Performing apfs_hfs_convert -x --verbose=0x400 /dev/disk10s2 Reporting post-conversion statistics A problem occurred during conversion from HFS to APFS APFS Converter exit code is 1 Aborted conversion in commit mode so will restore type Setting type of disk10s2 to CS Changing the physical disk partition type in shared mode Partition modification attempt count was 1 Not mounting APFS Volume Exiting conversion operations with error code -69860 Error: -69860: The underlying task reported failure on exit Underlying error: 1 ↩︎ Moar posts Encrypted RAID volumes in El Capitan Reminder: macOS system frameworks binaries are hidden (since Big Sur) tmutil is broken by SIP in Mojave Leave a Comment Cancel reply

items.title: USDB: Scaling Storage for Next-Generation Recommender Systems at ByteDance
items.articleText: Computer Science > Databases arXiv:2611.02618 (cs) [Submitted on 2 Nov 2026] Title: USDB: Scaling Storage for Next-Generation Recommender Systems at ByteDance Authors: Xiaoran Zhu , Jieming Cai , Weiping Yu , Xi Chen , Shu Cai , Jiahao Li , Yifan Xiao , Yan Deng , Yisha Zhou , Yu Lin , Shiru Ren , Siqiang Luo , Peng Xu , Junjun Chai View a PDF of the paper titled USDB: Scaling Storage for Next-Generation Recommender Systems at ByteDance, by Xiaoran Zhu and 13 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Recommendation models consume increasingly long, attribute-rich user histories, making small continuous updates and repeated large reads a central storage asymmetry. We present USDB, ByteDance's unified sequence storage practice for streaming and batch workloads. CascadeLSM time-based compaction stages materialize application-specific histories; differentiated replicas share persistent files; partial dumps reconstruct inference inputs from captured recent state and versioned history; and a hybrid columnar format accelerates projected reads. These designs reuse maintenance results across ingestion, inference, and training. Production migration records show 85.8% lower mean write latency, while normalized deployment accounting shows 42.1% lower infrastructure cost. Controlled comparisons with an Optimized RocksDB sequence baseline show faster long-history reads across projections and client loads. Aggregation pushdown sustains 8.5x the throughput of ordinary reads under a constrained receive budget. Production reconstruction and direct-file training results demonstrate how shared sequence maintenance supports fresh serving and repeated historical access. items.articleText:
## What's Changed
* `ollama launch claude` now applies the model's output token limit for Claude Code, so cloud models no longer run into the 128k default cap
* Cloud web search responses on `/api/chat` are now decoded correctly, including compressed responses
* OpenAI-compatible endpoints no longer override a model's packaged sampler defaults — clients that send no `temperature`/`top_p` get the model's own values instead of 1.0, matching `/api/chat`
* `/v1/responses` now preserves readable input content, including prior assistant refusals, instead of flattening it
* Ollama's app can now retry ChatGPT disconnect failures instead of leaving the connection in a broken state
* `ollama launch codex` verifies ChatGPT routing before configuring, and reports a clear error when routing is unavailable
* Faster top-k sampling on MLX for large vocabularies

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/ollama/ollama/compare/v0.40.13...v0.40.14

items.title: Ben Waters on the latest wireless charging strategies
items.summary: Ben Waters discusses opportunity charging, battery life, and the infrastructure needed to keep growing robot fleets running. The post Ben Waters on the latest wireless charging strategies appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: Wireless chargers are being deployed in a number of indoor and outdoor applications for charging the mobile robots. | Credit: WiBotic As robot fleets scale, charging becomes an operational challenge. Understanding how to optimize charging for fleets of mobile robots is key to getting the best performance from the fleet throughout the day. Ben Waters, CEO of WiBotic With growing deployments, charging is becoming more than a question of how long a battery lasts or how quickly it can recharge. Charging strategy can affect fleet uptime, facility infrastructure, maintenance requirements, and even the size of the batteries that robot manufacturers need to carry. Ben Waters, CEO of WiBotic , recently joined The Robot Report Podcast to discuss how those considerations are changing as robot fleets scale. He also discussed opportunity charging, the tradeoffs around fast charging, WiBotic’s move toward higher-power systems, and how charging data could help operators identify power problems. This is an excerpt from the podcast interview. Listen to the full audio anywhere you get your podcasts or online in the show notes . WiBotic expands beyond its traditional robotics markets What has changed recently at WiBotic, and how is the market maturing? Waters: Overall, WiBotic has diversified into a few different markets, but all the while, robotics has really been growing, as we all know, over the last last one to two years for sure. That was a big motivator for us to pursue getting into some adjacent markets. Take, for example, floor care , medical carts, space , and defense applications, all of which are markets that really use the same product as our longstanding robotics customers from a wireless charging, autonomous charging perspective. Flash-forward a year of focusing on that and putting all the internal operational, sales, and engineering teams in place to support different markets. Here we are a year and a half later, and robotics is booming everywhere you look, right? I mean, all of our legacy customers in robotics have had significant volume growth this year. We are seeing huge growth in automotive AMR adoption. We are seeing growth in outdoor robotic inspection for energy substations, and a lot of outdoor applications are growing. And then there’s the wild card of humanoids . Wireless charging is a really interesting dynamic in humanoids as far as what it can enable and how it can improve uptime and eliminate some of these Achilles’ heels issues that humanoids have around downtime. Opportunity charging changes the equation for large robot fleets As fleets of mobile robots grow, where does charging start creating operational friction? Waters: The big trend as charging relates to operational impact is what we’ve probably talked about before with Gene [Demaitre]. WiBotic has always looked at as a great opportunity for wireless charging. But, you know, it takes a while for fleets to get big enough for it to truly make sense. And I think we’re finally at that place. And what I’m referring to is opportunity charging. So it’s the concept of “Don’t just put the chargers on the sides of the factories.” And then when the battery on the robot gets to 20%, that robot might be on the far side of the factory. Now it’s got to drive 10 minutes while watching out for everything else and while being ignored by the fleet management for doing a task, even though it’s in an area where a task needs to get done, right? Because it has to go charge. That strategy, which is arguably easier to implement at a small scale, because you can truly just say, “If any one of these robots’ batteries hits 20%, stop and go drive to the charging station.” That’s fairly easy to implement. That gets really complicated, and that leads to a lot of unwanted downtime when the fleets start to get bigger. Even like fleets of 20 to 40, this becomes a bottleneck. We need to implement opportunity charging. And it doesn’t make sense to do opportunity charging with anything but wireless. Because if you did it with contacts, your robots would be hitting the contacts so many more times. And even if you had the world’s most strongest contact, it still would require maintenance at some point, times all of the chargers in your fleet. If the robot does a task and it’s got 10 seconds to sit there, well, a charging station should be positioned right where that robot naturally is going to sit. You could look at that as well. It’s only charging for 10 seconds, but if you do that often enough, it’s adding substantial energy back into the batteries across the fleet and allowing these things to run 24/7. You can completely eliminate that. Just allow the robots to stay in the loops where they’re operating when you employ opportunity charging. So that’s really the trend that we’ve been seeing and the demand we’ve been getting, and the main reason why companies are looking for wireless power. Submit your innovation now! Charging should be part of the robot design process How should companies think about charging during system design instead of treating it as an accessory at the end? Waters: If I boil it down to three things, I think companies should be thinking about power infrastructure. I’ll come back to a few details on these. Where are your electrical outlets, and how many of them do you have, and are they rated for enough power to handle all the chargers you want to deploy? So think about that up front. That bites people. We’ve seen a lot when you think about that too late. I think people are really questioning. How big of a battery do I need? Do I need a battery that supports an eight-hour runtime? Do I need a battery that supports super fast charging? In the world of batteries, most of these types of things trade off with each other. They might be overdesigning it. They might be adding way too much battery cost for what they really need, especially if they’re thinking about charging strategies. We still hear a lot of customers be like, “We need to charge these things as fast as humanly possible.” And we’re going to listen, and we’re going to assume the customers made the right choices for the right reasons. But sometimes, we do have a strong relationship with someone, we get into these topics. It’s not our job necessarily to push back, but we are curious battery guys, and we’re a friendly company to work with. So we sometimes ask: “Do you really want to charge at 3°C all the time? Have you seen a data sheet from the battery manufacturer that says what that’s gonna do to lifetime? Is that worth it?” And then the third thing for sure is maintenance. If you wait till you’ve already finished your design, and you’re starting to deploy and haven’t thought about those things, then almost surely, you will get bit by every one of those things within at least a couple of months, if not sooner. WiBotic develops chargers for outdoor robots, drones and humanoids As WiBotic moves into new applications, how have its products evolved? Waters: WiBotic has always really tried to think about what product serves the maximum number of customers and people, right? We’re not a consulting business where we customize every system. As far as developing circuits and certifying systems, we want to be a company that makes standard products and sells systems to customers that they can depend on that are supported and certified. We most recently launched in our 1 kW product family an IP65-rated version of the charger. When we first launched our 1 kW product a couple years ago, it was just available in our typical black box IP20 form factor. So we now have an IP65 form factor, which is really needed for outdoor applications and robotics. Really desirable from, you know, indoor applications like floor care where water and dust are very much parts of those systems. Right now, we are actively developing more around two areas of innovation. One is size and weight. We are seeing a lot of interest in drone applications. WiBotic certainly has had a long history with drones. We’re developing lightweight, high-power systems for drones, which just so happens to be kind of the same thing that humanoids need as well. The more mass you add to a humanoid, the more energy it has to spend because it’s balancing that mass. And there’s not a lot of space. So yeah, we’re focusing on a lot of small form-factor, high-power applications, as well as pushing the power of our current products up to a 3 kW level. With 25+ years of experience, including leadership roles at Adept Technology, Mike founded the Mobile Robot Guide (acquired by WTWH). He is a leading expert on Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs), physical AI, and RaaS business models, holding a Systems Engineering degree and an MBA. He can be reached at [email protected] . items.articleText: The new ISO 21423:2026 standard is intended to facilitate communications among different mobile robots. Source: mansyupasara AI, Adobe Stock As fleets of mobile robots grow, the need for interoperability among systems increases. The Association for Advancing Automation, or A3, yesterday published ISO 21423:2026, a new international standard for communications among industrial mobile robots, or IMRs, regardless of vendor or model. “Companies want to choose the robots that fit their applications and have those robots work together on the same floor,” stated Carole Franklin, director of standards development for robotics at A3. “Many leading industrial users of mobile robots have asked for an interoperability standard for years.” “Now, ISO 21423 gives manufacturers and users a common basis for communication across fleets, no matter where in the world their facility is located,” she added. “This standard can help companies expand automation with equipment from different vendors and make better use of the robots they already have.” ISO 21423 addresses IMR interoperability Developed by ISO Technical Committee 299, ISO 21423 Robotics – Industrial mobile robots – Communications and interoperability provides a common set of requirements for automated guided vehicles (AGVs ), autonomous mobile robots (AMRs ), and similar systems from different suppliers operating in the same facility. The new standard specifies how IMRs, fleet managers , and other equipment exchange information and request actions. Robots can share their location, speed, direction, condition, tasking and availability with one another, A3 explained. For end users, this means fewer cases of robots interfering with each other’s paths or path planning , which improves robot availability and system efficiency, asserted A3. A common protocol could increase competition in the market and support innovation, it said. One benefit of an ISO standard on this topic is that it can be adopted in countries all around the world. Submit your innovation now! Standard also covers communications with other systems ISO 21423 also covers communication with machines tended by robots; enterprise resource planning (ERP) tools; and industrial building systems such as lifts, automated doors, and alarms. People using or wearing mobile devices can share similar information, so their work can be coordinated alongside the robots. “ISO 21423 represents the first non-safety robot standard that A3 has helped produce, and highlights A3’s continued leadership in robotics standardization efforts,” said the Ann Arbor, Mich.-based organization. The standard is available at the A3 online store for $373. A3 members can purchase the document for $320. The Association for Advancing Automation is a leading global advocate for the benefits of automating. Members of A3 represent more than 1,500 manufacturers, component suppliers, systems integrators, end users, academic institutions, research groups, and consulting firms. items.title: Cities Worldwide Build and Scale AI Services With NVIDIA Physical and Agentic AI

items.articleText: Cities generate enormous amounts of data from cameras, sensors and operational systems, but turning it into useful action — for planning, maintenance and public services — remains a challenge. Physical and agentic AI offer new ways to close that gap, from digital twins for infrastructure planning to vision and service agents, while keeping local governments in control of how sensitive data is processed and used. Building on initiatives announced at GTC Berlin , NVIDIA and its partners are expanding physical AI and AI agents to cities worldwide. Shared computing infrastructure gives city departments, neighboring municipalities and local developers a common foundation to build on — extending services without each organization having to acquire and manage resources of their own. Agentic AI for Cities From resident services to vision agents, cities are adopting NVIDIA agentic AI to deliver faster, more responsive public services. City teams don’t need a massive infrastructure investment to get started building these AI services: depending on the workload, NVIDIA RTX workstations or a small GPU system may be enough. In Spain, 1MillionBot combines open source ALIA models trained at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center with NVIDIA Nemotron and other models in resident-service agents for Madrid Digital (Comunidad de Madrid), Administració Oberta de Catalunya and 150+ deployments across Spain, handling municipal procedures, appointment requests, urban-planning incidents and service inquiries. In the San Francisco Bay Area , LiveX is bringing its AI City vision to life with NVIDIA Cosmos world models and Nemotron open models, and Omniverse and Metropolis libraries on NVIDIA RTX PRO GPUs. The interactive, conversational AI hosts understand people’s needs, provide answers and take action, and can be tailored to local languages and service needs in airports, hospitals, local events and other public spaces. Vision AI agents can turn existing city camera feeds into operational insights, helping teams identify mobility and safety issues and coordinate emergency responses across city services. In Wrocław, Poland , K2K is building shared AI infrastructure using NVIDIA accelerated computing, NVIDIA Cosmos world reasoning models, and NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) to transform existing camera streams into actionable intelligence for mobility, safety and event response — using the same infrastructure across several city functions. In Malaysia , ITMAX bundles infrastructure and agentic AI applications into long-term managed services for cities, including for traffic management. Built with reference to Cosmos, Nemotron and the Metropolis VSS blueprint, ITMAX’s SamurAI V2 vision agents are scaling on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs to support 17,000+ cameras by 2027. ITMAX integrates TeraSim, an open source traffic simulation platform from Laplace Intelligence , to test signal timing, reducing peak-hour corridor travel times by up to 26%. Plan and Operate Critical Infrastructure With Digital Twins Beyond public-facing services, digital twins can help cities expedite infrastructure planning, minimizing disruption to local communities. City digital twins can also serve as a real-time operational simulation to facilitate faster decision-making. At Dangote’s Lekki refinery in Nigeria, Honeywell Technologies’ Forge Plant Cognition uses Nemotron-powered AI agents to understand operational data. A digital twin of the plant and its processes, built using Omniverse libraries, is also planned to support simulation and training. The platform, built on Dell PowerEdge servers with NVIDIA RTX PRO accelerators, helps operators identify bottlenecks, anticipate equipment and process issues, and optimize plant performance. In Taiwan , Linker Vision and Dutch architecture firm MVRDV are using NVIDIA Omniverse and Nemotron to build environmental, social and governance agents that can assess the environmental impact of various urban planning scenarios, simulating 15-year outcomes of an urban forest canopy in 10 minutes — increasing design iteration speed from two weeks per iteration to less than an hour. Build a Broader Local AI Ecosystem Cities can extend AI to more services by building on infrastructure already in place and adding capacity. Shared resources and managed services can help extend those capabilities across departments and municipalities. At Morocco’s Tanger Med port, Cires Technologies is expanding a sovereign AI factory for planned applications in worker safety, congestion analysis, cargo routing and port operations. Cires Technologies is also building an ecosystem of application providers to develop local models and applications for ports and cities. Beyond city services, Barcelona Supercomputing Center’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme gives startups access to sovereign computing, technical support and training. BSC AI Factory also supports research and innovation for startups — spanning agriculture, medical imaging, knowledge access and speech services. Learn how NVIDIA and its ecosystem are bringing physical AI, agentic AI and local AI factories to cities worldwide at Smart City Expo World Congress, running Nov. 3-5 in Barcelona, where NVIDIA Vice President of EMEA Paolo Guglielmini will deliver a keynote address followed by a panel moderated by Charbel Aoun, director of smart city and spaces for EMEA at NVIDIA. report.cross_insight: - 해석: 대규모 로봇 플릿 운영 효율화 측면에서 WiBotic의 무선 기회 충전 제안과 ISO 21423:2026 상호운용성 표준 제정은 현장 내 이동 병목 및 경로 간섭 문제를 줄이려는 공통된 산업적 요구를 반영합니다 [19, 20]
report.section_robotics:
- **ROS 2 Rolling rclcpp 내장 토픽 통계 제거**: ROS 2 Rolling 및 향후 Makoa Mata-mata(2027년 5월 예정)에서 rclcpp 내장 토픽 통계와 core 패키지 libstatistics_collector가 삭제되었습니다. C++ 토픽 통계 API를 사용하는 기존 코드는 Rolling 환경에서 컴파일되지 않으며 /statistics 토픽 발행도 중단됩니다 [1]
- **Microduck MuJoCo-ROS 2 통합 라이브러리**: Pollen Robotics의 Microduck 2족 보행 로봇 학습 정책을 수정 없이 MuJoCo에서 구동하고 표준 ROS 2 인터페이스로 제어하는 환경이 공개되었습니다. 킥, 구르기, 물건 집기, 앉기/일어서기 등 기존 스킬이 ROS 2 서비스 형태로 제공됩니다 [4]
report.section_devtools:
- **Qwen 3.8 27B 신경망 가중치 직접 해석 실험**: LLM이 신경망 가중치를 직접 분석·수정하는 Weight-Space Programming 개념을 통해, Qwen 3.8 27B 로컬 모델이 도구 지원 없이 부동소수점 가중치 텍스트만으로 팩맨, 퐁, 브레이크아웃 정책망을 식별한 작성자의 실험 결과가 공유되었습니다 [14]
- **Ollama v0.40.14**: ollama launch claude 실행 시 Claude Code에 맞춰 모델 출력 토큰 제한이 적용되도록 수정되었으며, OpenAI 호환 엔드포인트에서 클라이언트가 temperature나 top_p를 미지정할 경우 모델 고유 기본값을 유지하도록 개선되었습니다 [18]
report.section_industry:
- **WiBotic 무선 기회 충전 전략**: 플릿 규모 확대에 따른 충전소 이동 병목을 줄이기 위해 대기 위치에서 짧게 충전하는 기회 충전 방식과 1kW IP65 무선 충전기를 제시했으며, 3kW급 시스템을 개발 중이라고 밝혔습니다 [19]

entries.title: ROS 2 Rolling에서 rclcpp 내장 토픽 통계 및 libstatistics_collector 제거
entries.reason: ROS 2 차기 배포판 Makoa Mata-mata 및 Rolling에서 C++ 토픽 통계 API가 완전히 제거되어 빌드 실패가 발생할 수 있으므로, ros2_tracing 기반 대체 방안과 변경 사항을 사전에 확인해야 합니다.

facts.statement: ROS 2 Rolling 및 향후 Makoa Mata-mata(2027년 5월 예정)에서 rclcpp의 내장 토픽 통계 구현과 core 패키지인 libstatistics_collector가 제거되었습니다.
facts.quote: built-in topic statistics have been removed from rclcpp , and libstatistics_collector is no longer part of the ROS 2 core.

facts.statement: C++ 토픽 통계 API를 사용하는 기존 코드는 Rolling 환경에서 더 이상 컴파일되지 않으며, /statistics 토픽을 통한 데이터 발행도 중단됩니다.
facts.quote: In that case your code will no longer compile against Rolling .

prerelease_exception.reason: Rolling 및 Makoa Mata-mata 배포판에서 NodeOptions와 SubscriptionOptions 내 topic_statistics API가 완전히 삭제되어 기존 빌드가 중단되는 호환성 단절이 발생함.

facts.statement: 새로운 통합 도구는 microduck-policies의 기존 정책을 수정하지 않고 MuJoCo 환경에서 구동할 수 있도록 지원합니다.
facts.quote: The integration allows Microduck policies to run in MuJoCo while exposing the simulated robot through standard ROS 2 interfaces.

facts.quote: Skill integration: Existing skills such as kicks, roulade, ground pick, and sit/stand are exposed as ROS 2 services.

entries.title: 로컬 환경 Qwen 3.8 27B 모델의 신경망 가중치 직접 해석(Weight-Space Programming) 실험
entries.reason: 별도의 도구나 코드 실행 없이 신경망의 부동소수점 가중치 텍스트만으로 로컬 LLM이 강화학습 정책망의 대상 게임을 식별할 수 있음을 확인한 개발자 실험입니다.

facts.statement: 논문에서 정의된 Weight-Space Programming 개념을 바탕으로, Qwen 3.8 27B 로컬 모델은 도구 지원 없이 가중치 텍스트만으로 팩맨, 퐁, 브레이크아웃 정책망을 식별했습니다.
facts.quote: Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze

facts.statement: 해당 연구는 LLM이 신경망 가중치를 직접 분석하고 수정하는 기법을 가리켜 Weight-Space Programming으로 명명했습니다.
facts.quote: coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights

- **ROS 2 Rolling rclcpp 내장 토픽 통계 제거**: ROS 2 Rolling 및 향후 Makoa Mata-mata(2027년 5월 예정)에서 rclcpp 내장 토픽 통계와 core 패키지 libstatistics_collector가 삭제되었습니다. C++ 토픽 통계 API를 사용하는 기존 코드는 Rolling 환경에서 컴파일되지 않으며 /statistics 토픽 발행도 중단됩니다 [1].
- **Microduck MuJoCo-ROS 2 통합 라이브러리**: Pollen Robotics의 Microduck 2족 보행 로봇 학습 정책을 수정 없이 MuJoCo에서 구동하고 표준 ROS 2 인터페이스로 제어하는 환경이 공개되었습니다. 킥, 구르기, 물건 집기, 앉기/일어서기 등 기존 스킬이 ROS 2 서비스 형태로 제공됩니다 [4].
draft.section_devtools:
- **Qwen 3.8 27B 신경망 가중치 직접 해석 실험**: LLM이 신경망 가중치를 직접 분석·수정하는 Weight-Space Programming 개념을 통해, Qwen 3.8 27B 로컬 모델이 도구 지원 없이 부동소수점 가중치 텍스트만으로 팩맨, 퐁, 브레이크아웃 정책망을 식별한 작성자의 실험 결과가 공유되었습니다 [14].
- **Ollama v0.40.14**: ollama launch claude 실행 시 Claude Code에 맞춰 모델 출력 토큰 제한이 적용되도록 수정되었습니다. OpenAI 호환 엔드포인트에서 클라이언트가 temperature나 top_p를 지정하지 않을 경우 강제로 1.0으로 덮어쓰지 않고 모델 자체 기본값을 적용합니다 [18].
draft.section_industry:
- **WiBotic 무선 기회 충전 전략**: 플릿 규모 확대에 따른 충전소 이동 병목을 줄이기 위해 대기 위치에서 짧게 충전하는 기회 충전 방식과 1kW IP65 무선 충전기를 제시했으며, 3kW급 시스템을 개발 중이라고 밝혔습니다 [19].
- **ISO 21423:2026 모바일 로봇 통신 표준**: A3와 ISO TC 299가 서로 다른 제조사의 산업용 모바일 로봇(IMR) 간 통신을 조율하는 국제 표준 ISO 21423:2026을 발표했습니다. 로봇 간 위치, 속도, 상태, 작업 정보를 상호 교환해 경로 간섭을 최소화하도록 지원합니다 [20].

What changed The following PRs were merged on October 5, 2026: ros2/rclcpp#3203 : removes the topic statistics implementation from rclcpp , rclcpp_lifecycle and rclcpp_components ros2/ros2#1878 : removes libstatistics_collector from ros2.repos ros2/demos#812 : removes the topic_statistics_demo package ros2/examples#476 : removes the MinimalSubscriberWithTopicStatistics example ros2/ros2_documentation#7245 : removes the topic statistics tutorial and concept pages from the Rolling docs Why Hardly anyone was using it. Recent bug reports suggested the feature saw very little real-world use. There’s a better way to get this data. At ROSCon we discussed providing an interface so a third-party package could plug the old behavior back in. We decided not to: tooling that hooks into the existing tracepoints (tracetools / ros2_tracing ) can collect the same information without adding code and cost to every subscription. Faster builds. rclcpp no longer depends on libstatistics_collector and statistics_msgs , and fewer templates end up in every subscription. Compiling a simple node with one publisher and one subscription went from 6.32 s to 4.91 s (about 22% faster, measured on a Ryzen 9900X). Overall, the change removes around 2,400 lines of code. Am I affected? Only if you use the C++ topic statistics API. In that case your code will no longer compile against Rolling . These are removed: Removed Where NodeOptions::enable_topic_statistics() (getter and setter) rclcpp/node_options.hpp SubscriptionOptions::topic_stats_options (TopicStatisticsOptions : state , publish_topic , publish_period , qos ) rclcpp/subscription_options.hpp rclcpp::TopicStatisticsState rclcpp/topic_statistics_state.hpp rclcpp::topic_statistics::SubscriptionTopicStatistics rclcpp/topic_statistics/subscription_topic_statistics.hpp NodeBaseInterface::get_enable_topic_statistics_default() , and the enable_topic_statistics_default argument of the NodeBase constructor rclcpp/node_interfaces/ The enable_topic_statistics extra argument when loading a component rclcpp_components Note that the last two items also affect you if you implement your own NodeBaseInterface , or if your launch files pass enable_topic_statistics as an extra argument to a composable node. Also, nothing publishes on the /statistics topic anymore. Tools or dashboards that subscribe to it will stop receiving data. The statistics_msgs message package itself is not removed. It lives in rcl_interfaces , so existing tools that use those messages keep building. How to migrate Remove the API calls listed above. For most users that’s deleting options.topic_stats_options.state = rclcpp::TopicStatisticsState::Enable; (or .enable_topic_statistics(true) ) and the related includes. Collect statistics from tracepoints instead. rclcpp already emits tracepoints on every publish and every subscription callback, which give you message rates, periods and latencies without changing your nodes: ros2_tracing to record traces and analyze them offline. Community tools built on the same instrumentation are already appearing. For example, ros2_pulse reports live topic rates, can export to Prometheus and Grafana, and can even publish statistics_msgs on /statistics if you have tooling that depends on it. Need it on older distros? Nothing changes for Humble, Jazzy, Kilted or Lyrical: topic statistics are still there. The removal only applies to Rolling and to Makoa Mata-mata onwards. Feedback welcome During review, @tomoyafujita raised good points: whether this should have gone through a deprecation period first, and whether a longer-term statistics hook should live at the rcl level, so rclpy and other client libraries, plus services and actions, could share one mechanism. We went with a direct removal because the feature had so few users and we’re early in the Makoa cycle, which leaves plenty of time to react before the release. If you depend on topic statistics in production, please reply here. We’d like to hear what you’re using it for, so we can point you to the right replacement or document a migration path. Thanks to @jmachowinski for driving this cleanup, and to everyone who reviewed it and joined the discussion at ROSCon. Now you can configure its test environment and define the key user journeys it tests. Try it for free Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too 3rd November 2026 Yesterday’s hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Weight-Space Programming Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models. spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use. I’m going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two. The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games—Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it’s an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question: The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response. The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games: breakout/prompt.txt freeway/prompt.txt pacman/prompt.txt pong/prompt.txt I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others. Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this: llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \ -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here’s what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro , which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens. But how about Qwen 3.8 27B ? That’s still my favorite model to run on my own laptop—it’s just 17GB (I use this version ) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025. I fired up LM Studio , ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command: LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \ llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \ -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b (I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue .) After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here’s the reasoning trace ): Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets. Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards. Confidence: 72% This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong (reasoning ) in 1h 4m 54s: Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object. Description: The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized. Confidence: 75% And Breakout (reasoning ) in 52m 25s: Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game. Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty. Confidence: 88% Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn’t surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here’s that transcript —Qwen thought it was “A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally”. The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here’s a sample: What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let’s list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right? That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort. It’s a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I’ve seen around it does not feel justified. I’m not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways. selectedItems.articleText:
## What's Changed
* `ollama launch claude` now applies the model's output token limit for Claude Code, so cloud models no longer run into the 128k default cap
* Cloud web search responses on `/api/chat` are now decoded correctly, including compressed responses
* OpenAI-compatible endpoints no longer override a model's packaged sampler defaults — clients that send no `temperature`/`top_p` get the model's own values instead of 1.0, matching `/api/chat`
* `/v1/responses` now preserves readable input content, including prior assistant refusals, instead of flattening it
* Ollama's app can now retry ChatGPT disconnect failures instead of leaving the connection in a broken state
* `ollama launch codex` verifies ChatGPT routing before configuring, and reports a clear error when routing is unavailable
* Faster top-k sampling on MLX for large vocabularies

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/ollama/ollama/compare/v0.40.13...v0.40.14

selectedItems.articleText: Wireless chargers are being deployed in a number of indoor and outdoor applications for charging the mobile robots. | Credit: WiBotic As robot fleets scale, charging becomes an operational challenge. Understanding how to optimize charging for fleets of mobile robots is key to getting the best performance from the fleet throughout the day. Ben Waters, CEO of WiBotic With growing deployments, charging is becoming more than a question of how long a battery lasts or how quickly it can recharge. Charging strategy can affect fleet uptime, facility infrastructure, maintenance requirements, and even the size of the batteries that robot manufacturers need to carry. Ben Waters, CEO of WiBotic , recently joined The Robot Report Podcast to discuss how those considerations are changing as robot fleets scale. He also discussed opportunity charging, the tradeoffs around fast charging, WiBotic’s move toward higher-power systems, and how charging data could help operators identify power problems. This is an excerpt from the podcast interview. Listen to the full audio anywhere you get your podcasts or online in the show notes . WiBotic expands beyond its traditional robotics markets What has changed recently at WiBotic, and how is the market maturing? Waters: Overall, WiBotic has diversified into a few different markets, but all the while, robotics has really been growing, as we all know, over the last last one to two years for sure. That was a big motivator for us to pursue getting into some adjacent markets. Take, for example, floor care , medical carts, space , and defense applications, all of which are markets that really use the same product as our longstanding robotics customers from a wireless charging, autonomous charging perspective. Flash-forward a year of focusing on that and putting all the internal operational, sales, and engineering teams in place to support different markets. Here we are a year and a half later, and robotics is booming everywhere you look, right? I mean, all of our legacy customers in robotics have had significant volume growth this year. We are seeing huge growth in automotive AMR adoption. We are seeing growth in outdoor robotic inspection for energy substations, and a lot of outdoor applications are growing. And then there’s the wild card of humanoids . Wireless charging is a really interesting dynamic in humanoids as far as what it can enable and how it can improve uptime and eliminate some of these Achilles’ heels issues that humanoids have around downtime. Opportunity charging changes the equation for large robot fleets As fleets of mobile robots grow, where does charging start creating operational friction? Waters: The big trend as charging relates to operational impact is what we’ve probably talked about before with Gene [Demaitre]. WiBotic has always looked at as a great opportunity for wireless charging. But, you know, it takes a while for fleets to get big enough for it to truly make sense. And I think we’re finally at that place. And what I’m referring to is opportunity charging. So it’s the concept of “Don’t just put the chargers on the sides of the factories.” And then when the battery on the robot gets to 20%, that robot might be on the far side of the factory. Now it’s got to drive 10 minutes while watching out for everything else and while being ignored by the fleet management for doing a task, even though it’s in an area where a task needs to get done, right? Because it has to go charge. That strategy, which is arguably easier to implement at a small scale, because you can truly just say, “If any one of these robots’ batteries hits 20%, stop and go drive to the charging station.” That’s fairly easy to implement. That gets really complicated, and that leads to a lot of unwanted downtime when the fleets start to get bigger. Even like fleets of 20 to 40, this becomes a bottleneck. We need to implement opportunity charging. And it doesn’t make sense to do opportunity charging with anything but wireless. Because if you did it with contacts, your robots would be hitting the contacts so many more times. And even if you had the world’s most strongest contact, it still would require maintenance at some point, times all of the chargers in your fleet. If the robot does a task and it’s got 10 seconds to sit there, well, a charging station should be positioned right where that robot naturally is going to sit. You could look at that as well. It’s only charging for 10 seconds, but if you do that often enough, it’s adding substantial energy back into the batteries across the fleet and allowing these things to run 24/7. You can completely eliminate that. Just allow the robots to stay in the loops where they’re operating when you employ opportunity charging. So that’s really the trend that we’ve been seeing and the demand we’ve been getting, and the main reason why companies are looking for wireless power. Submit your innovation now! Charging should be part of the robot design process How should companies think about charging during system design instead of treating it as an accessory at the end? Waters: If I boil it down to three things, I think companies should be thinking about power infrastructure. I’ll come back to a few details on these. Where are your electrical outlets, and how many of them do you have, and are they rated for enough power to handle all the chargers you want to deploy? So think about that up front. That bites people. We’ve seen a lot when you think about that too late. I think people are really questioning. How big of a battery do I need? Do I need a battery that supports an eight-hour runtime? Do I need a battery that supports super fast charging? In the world of batteries, most of these types of things trade off with each other. They might be overdesigning it. They might be adding way too much battery cost for what they really need, especially if they’re thinking about charging strategies. We still hear a lot of customers be like, “We need to charge these things as fast as humanly possible.” And we’re going to listen, and we’re going to assume the customers made the right choices for the right reasons. But sometimes, we do have a strong relationship with someone, we get into these topics. It’s not our job necessarily to push back, but we are curious battery guys, and we’re a friendly company to work with. So we sometimes ask: “Do you really want to charge at 3°C all the time? Have you seen a data sheet from the battery manufacturer that says what that’s gonna do to lifetime? Is that worth it?” And then the third thing for sure is maintenance. If you wait till you’ve already finished your design, and you’re starting to deploy and haven’t thought about those things, then almost surely, you will get bit by every one of those things within at least a couple of months, if not sooner. WiBotic develops chargers for outdoor robots, drones and humanoids As WiBotic moves into new applications, how have its products evolved? Waters: WiBotic has always really tried to think about what product serves the maximum number of customers and people, right? We’re not a consulting business where we customize every system. As far as developing circuits and certifying systems, we want to be a company that makes standard products and sells systems to customers that they can depend on that are supported and certified. We most recently launched in our 1 kW product family an IP65-rated version of the charger. When we first launched our 1 kW product a couple years ago, it was just available in our typical black box IP20 form factor. So we now have an IP65 form factor, which is really needed for outdoor applications and robotics. Really desirable from, you know, indoor applications like floor care where water and dust are very much parts of those systems. Right now, we are actively developing more around two areas of innovation. One is size and weight. We are seeing a lot of interest in drone applications. WiBotic certainly has had a long history with drones. We’re developing lightweight, high-power systems for drones, which just so happens to be kind of the same thing that humanoids need as well. The more mass you add to a humanoid, the more energy it has to spend because it’s balancing that mass. And there’s not a lot of space. So yeah, we’re focusing on a lot of small form-factor, high-power applications, as well as pushing the power of our current products up to a 3 kW level. selectedItems.title: New ISO interoperability standard covers collaboration among mobile robots from multiple vendors
selectedItems.summary: The ISO 21423:2026 interoperability standard is intended to allow mobile robots from multiple vendors to communicate and coordinate. The post New ISO interoperability standard covers collaboration among mobile robots from multiple vendors appeared first on The Robot Report .
selectedItems.articleText: The new ISO 21423:2026 standard is intended to facilitate communications among different mobile robots. Source: mansyupasara AI, Adobe Stock As fleets of mobile robots grow, the need for interoperability among systems increases. The Association for Advancing Automation, or A3, yesterday published ISO 21423:2026, a new international standard for communications among industrial mobile robots, or IMRs, regardless of vendor or model. “Companies want to choose the robots that fit their applications and have those robots work together on the same floor,” stated Carole Franklin, director of standards development for robotics at A3. “Many leading industrial users of mobile robots have asked for an interoperability standard for years.” “Now, ISO 21423 gives manufacturers and users a common basis for communication across fleets, no matter where in the world their facility is located,” she added. “This standard can help companies expand automation with equipment from different vendors and make better use of the robots they already have.” ISO 21423 addresses IMR interoperability Developed by ISO Technical Committee 299, ISO 21423 Robotics – Industrial mobile robots – Communications and interoperability provides a common set of requirements for automated guided vehicles (AGVs ), autonomous mobile robots (AMRs ), and similar systems from different suppliers operating in the same facility. The new standard specifies how IMRs, fleet managers , and other equipment exchange information and request actions. Robots can share their location, speed, direction, condition, tasking and availability with one another, A3 explained. For end users, this means fewer cases of robots interfering with each other’s paths or path planning , which improves robot availability and system efficiency, asserted A3. A common protocol could increase competition in the market and support innovation, it said. One benefit of an ISO standard on this topic is that it can be adopted in countries all around the world. Submit your innovation now! Standard also covers communications with other systems ISO 21423 also covers communication with machines tended by robots; enterprise resource planning (ERP) tools; and industrial building systems such as lifts, automated doors, and alarms. People using or wearing mobile devices can share similar information, so their work can be coordinated alongside the robots. “ISO 21423 represents the first non-safety robot standard that A3 has helped produce, and highlights A3’s continued leadership in robotics standardization efforts,” said the Ann Arbor, Mich.-based organization. The standard is available at the A3 online store for $373. A3 members can purchase the document for $320. The Association for Advancing Automation is a leading global advocate for the benefits of automating. Members of A3 represent more than 1,500 manufacturers, component suppliers, systems integrators, end users, academic institutions, research groups, and consulting firms.
